lessons.title: How Regulators Responded: SEBI, RBI, and the Exchanges

body.text: Almost every rule that protects you today was written after someone lost money. Knowing which safety nets exist, and which risks they will never cover, is part of being a responsible investor.

children.text: Each crash in this course ended with new rules. This lesson brings those reforms up to date and turns them into a practical map. You will see what SEBI, RBI and the exchanges each do in a crisis, how recent failures such as Karvy Stock Broking, IL&FS and Yes Bank reshaped the protections around your shares, deposits and mutual funds, and, just as importantly, which risks no regulator can protect you from.
Three Guardians, Three Jobs

body.caption: Who Protects What in India's Financial System
headers: Where You Saw It in This Course

cells: SEBI
Stock markets, brokers, depositories, mutual funds, listed companies and investment advisers
Investigations, trading bans, margin rules, new disclosure and investor protection rules
Statutory powers in 1992, reforms after the 2001 crash, F&O and finfluencer rules
RBI
Banks, non-bank lenders (NBFCs), interest rates, liquidity and the currency
Rate cuts, liquidity injections, special lending windows, bank moratoriums and rescues
Pre-2008 risk weights, 2008 and 2020 rate cuts, ICICI Bank statement, Yes Bank rescue
Stock exchanges and clearing corporations
Trading, settlement and surveillance on NSE and BSE
Circuit breakers, price bands, surveillance frameworks, settlement guarantees, investor protection funds
Circuit breakers in 2001 and 2020, the 2012 flash crash, ASM and GSM frameworks
DICGC
Deposit insurance for bank depositors
Paying insured depositors when a bank fails or is restricted
Deposit insurance of up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank

columns.label: Firefighting (During a Crisis)
points: Cutting interest rates and releasing liquidity
Halting trading through market-wide circuit breakers
Opening special lending windows, such as for mutual funds in 2008 and 2020
Placing a troubled bank under moratorium and arranging a rescue
Goal: stop panic from turning into collapse

columns.label: Rebuilding (After a Crisis)
points: Writing new rules to close the gap that was exploited
Changing how shares, money and collateral are held
Tightening leverage limits and disclosure requirements
Strengthening investor compensation and complaint systems
Goal: make the same failure harder to repeat

body.title: Firefighting or Rebuilding?
body.question: Which of these is a rebuilding response rather than a firefighting response?
options: RBI cutting the repo rate by 75 basis points in March 2020
NSE halting trading for 45 minutes after a 10% index fall
SEBI requiring shares to stay in investors' own demat accounts when pledged for margin, after a broker misused client securities
RBI opening a special liquidity window for mutual funds facing redemptions
body.explanation: The new margin pledge system was a structural rule change made after the Karvy episode, designed to stop a whole category of misuse from happening again. The other three are emergency measures used during a crisis to calm panic and keep money flowing.

children.text: Your Shares: From Karvy to Direct Payout

markDefs.definition: A legal authorisation that allowed a broker to operate a client's demat account, such as moving shares to settle trades. It was later replaced by a narrower, standardised instruction.

children.text: In November 2019, SEBI found that Karvy Stock Broking had transferred securities worth about ₹2,300 crore belonging to more than 95,000 clients into its own account, misusing the
power of attorney

clients had given it, and had pledged those shares to raise money. SEBI barred Karvy from taking new clients on 22 November 2019, and NSE later declared it a defaulter. For investors, the shock was realising that shares sitting in a broker-linked account were not as safe as they believed. A series of reforms followed.

body.title: How the Safety Net Around Your Shares and Money Was Rebuilt

events.title: The Karvy Shock
events.description: SEBI finds Karvy Stock Broking misused about ₹2,300 crore of client securities and bars it from taking new clients.

events.title: Shares Stay in Your Demat
events.description: A new margin pledge system takes effect. Shares pledged for margin stay in the client's own demat account, with the pledge created in favour of the broker, instead of being transferred to the broker.

events.title: Online Dispute Resolution
events.description: SEBI launches a common online portal for conciliation and arbitration of disputes with brokers, depository participants and other market entities.

events.title: SCORES 2.0
events.description: SEBI's upgraded complaint system sets a uniform 21 day timeline for resolving investor complaints, with automatic routing and escalation.

events.title: Higher Compensation Ceiling
events.description: NSE raises the maximum payable to an investor from its Investor Protection Fund from ₹25 lakh to ₹35 lakh, for claims against defaulting brokers.

events.title: Direct Payout of Shares
events.description: Shares bought by clients are credited directly from the clearing corporation to the client's demat account, rather than passing through the broker's pool account.

events.title: Money Stays in Your Bank
events.description: Large brokers must offer either a UPI-based block mechanism, where funds stay in your bank account until a trade settles, or a 3-in-1 account linking bank, trading and demat accounts.

stats.label: NSE IPF Ceiling per Investor
stats.context: Up about 40% from ₹25 lakh, for claims against defaulters after 13 August 2024

body.text: Notice the direction of every reform in that timeline. Each one reduces the time your shares or money spend in someone else's hands. The safest asset is one that sits in an account in your own name, moves only with your authorisation, and can be checked independently of your broker.

children.text: Your Bank Deposits: DICGC and the 90 Day Promise

Deposit insurance in India was stuck at ₹1 lakh per depositor for decades. After depositors of Punjab and Maharashtra Co-operative (PMC) Bank were caught by withdrawal restrictions in 2019, the limit was raised 5 times to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, with effect from 4 February 2020. A 2021 amendment to the DICGC Act went further: if RBI places a bank under restrictions or a moratorium, insured depositors are to receive interim payment of up to ₹5 lakh within 90 days, instead of waiting years for the bank to be liquidated.

The Yes Bank crisis showed how RBI now handles a large troubled private bank. On 5 March 2020, RBI imposed a moratorium, capping withdrawals at ₹50,000 per depositor. Within days, a reconstruction scheme was in place, with State Bank of India investing ₹7,250 crore for a stake of up to 49%. The restrictions were lifted within weeks, and depositors did not lose their money.

body.latex: \text{Insured Amount in Each Bank} = \min(\text{Total Deposits in That Bank}, \; \text{₹5 lakh})
body.caption: Cover applies per depositor per bank, combining principal and interest across savings, current and fixed deposit accounts held in the same capacity.

body.title: Your Turn: How Much Is Uninsured?
body.prompt: Anita holds a ₹2 lakh savings account and a ₹7 lakh fixed deposit in Bank A, and a ₹3 lakh savings account in Bank B, all in her own name. Using DICGC cover of ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, how much of her money, in ₹ lakh, is not covered by deposit insurance? Ignore interest.
body.explanation: Bank A holds ₹9 lakh in total, but cover is capped at ₹5 lakh per bank, so ₹4 lakh is uninsured. Bank B holds ₹3 lakh, which is fully covered. Anita's uninsured amount is ₹4 lakh. Moving ₹4 lakh of the fixed deposit to a third bank when it matures would bring all ₹12 lakh within insured limits.

children.text: Your Mutual Funds and Lenders: After IL&FS

markDefs.definition: Separating a defaulted or downgraded bond into a separate portfolio within a debt fund, so that new investors do not buy into it and existing investors receive any later recovery.

children.text: In 2018, Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services (IL&FS), a large infrastructure lender with about ₹91,000 crore of debt, began defaulting. Debt mutual funds holding its bonds saw sudden losses, and credit to non-bank lenders tightened sharply. Two reforms followed. In December 2018, SEBI allowed debt mutual funds to use
side pocketing

, so that a single bad bond no longer contaminates the entire fund. And in October 2021, RBI introduced scale-based regulation for NBFCs, applying stricter rules to the largest and most interconnected non-bank lenders, effective from October 2022.

As you saw in Lesson 1.3, Franklin Templeton's 2020 wind-up showed that liquidity risk in debt funds had not disappeared. Investors eventually recovered more than they had invested, but lost access to their money for a long time. Regulation reduces the damage of such events; it does not eliminate the risk.
Your Trading: Curbing Leverage and Bad Advice

markDefs.definition: Financial influencers who give investment advice or stock tips on social media. Those who are not registered with SEBI as advisers or research analysts are not permitted to give personalised recommendations or claim returns.

children.text: SEBI's studies showing that about 93% of individual F&O traders lost money between FY22 and FY24 led to a package of measures announced on 1 October 2024. At the same time, SEBI moved against a new source of risk: unregistered
finfluencers

body.caption: Recent SEBI Responses to Retail Trading Risks

cells: Excessive leverage in intraday trading
Peak margin rules, fully in force from September 2021
Intraday leverage limited to about 5x
Heavy retail losses in index options
Minimum index derivative contract size raised from ₹5 to 10 lakh to ₹15 to 20 lakh, from 20 November 2024
Larger lot sizes, such as Nifty moving from 50 to 75 units per lot, raising the capital needed per trade
Expiry-day speculation
Each exchange limited to weekly expiry contracts on one benchmark index, from 20 November 2024
Fewer weekly expiries to trade
Buying options on credit
Upfront collection of option premium from buyers, from 1 February 2025
Option buyers must pay the full premium before trading
Stock tips from unregistered influencers
SEBI-regulated entities barred from associating with unregistered finfluencers, from August 2024
Brokers and platforms can no longer pay or partner with unregistered tip givers

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: SEBI's online complaint platform, upgraded to version 2.0 in April 2024 with a 21 day resolution timeline, is called ___.
body.explanation: SCORES stands for SEBI Complaints Redress System. If a broker, depository participant, mutual fund or listed company does not resolve your complaint, you can escalate it there, and use the Online Dispute Resolution portal for conciliation or arbitration if needed.

children.text: What No Regulator Can Protect You From

body.text: Regulators protect the plumbing of the market: that trades settle, that your shares and deposits are not stolen, that companies disclose information and that leverage is limited. They do not protect you from losing money on a bad investment, from buying at the top of a bubble, or from your own panic in a crash.

columns.label: What the System Protects
points: Your shares held in your own demat account
Bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank
Settlement of trades through the clearing corporation
Compensation, within limits, if a broker defaults
A formal complaint and dispute resolution process

columns.label: What It Does Not Protect
points: Falls in the price of shares or mutual funds you own
Losses from overpaying in a bubble or a hyped IPO
Losses from your own leverage, F&O trades or MTF positions
Money given to unregistered advisers or "guaranteed return" schemes
The cost of selling in panic during a crash

body.title: Why Regulators Always Seem to Fight the Last War

children.text: Look back at this course and a pattern appears. Margin limits came after 1929, circuit breakers after 1987, demat after 1992, rolling settlement after 2001, the new pledge system after Karvy, side pocketing after IL&FS. Regulation is usually a response to the last failure.
Why:
it is hard to justify strict rules against a risk that has not yet caused visible harm, especially during a boom when everyone is making money.
The consequence:
the next crisis often comes from a new direction, such as a new product, a new platform or a new form of leverage.
What it means for you:
assume that the newest, fastest growing and least understood corner of the market is the one with the weakest rules.

body.title: Is My Broker Safe?
body.scenario: Priya reads a news report that her discount broker is under SEBI investigation for alleged lapses in handling client funds. She has ₹6 lakh of shares and ₹40,000 of unused cash sitting with the broker. Her first instinct is to sell all her shares immediately and withdraw everything.
body.prompt: What protections apply to Priya's shares and cash, and what practical steps should she take before doing anything drastic?
body.modelAnswer: Selling her shares would be the wrong first move, because selling does not make them safer; it only turns them into cash that also sits with the broker for a while. Under today's rules, Priya's shares are held in a demat account in her own name with a depository, NSDL or CDSL, not in the broker's account. Since November 2024, shares she buys are credited directly to her demat account. If she has pledged shares for margin, they still remain in her demat account under the pledge system introduced in September 2020. Her practical steps: first, check her holdings independently, using the consolidated account statement from NSDL or CDSL, or the depository's own app, to confirm every share is in her name. Second, check for any pledges she did not authorise. Third, withdraw the unused ₹40,000 to her bank account, since idle cash with a broker is more exposed than shares in her demat. Fourth, if she remains uncomfortable, she can transfer her shares to a demat account with another broker without selling them. If anything is missing, she should complain to the broker, escalate through SEBI's SCORES platform, and, if the broker is ever declared a defaulter, file a claim with the exchange's investor protection fund within the specified time. An investigation is a reason to verify, not a reason to panic.

body.title: Audit Your Own Safety Nets
steps: Download your latest consolidated account statement from NSDL or CDSL and match every holding with your broker app
Check for any pledges on your shares that you did not personally authorise
Review how much unused cash is lying with your broker, and withdraw what you do not need for trading
Add up your deposits in each bank, including fixed deposits, and check them against the ₹5 lakh DICGC limit
Before following any stock tip from social media, check whether the person is registered with SEBI as an investment adviser or research analyst
Confirm that nominees are registered on your demat account, mutual fund folios and bank accounts
Bookmark SEBI's SCORES portal so you know where to escalate a complaint if you ever need to

body.label: SEBI SCORES: Complaint Redress System
body.description: SEBI's official platform for lodging complaints against brokers, depository participants, mutual funds, listed companies and other regulated entities, with a 21 day resolution timeline.

cards.definition: Since September 2020, shares pledged for margin stay in the client's own demat account with a pledge in favour of the broker.
Since November 2024, shares bought are credited directly from the clearing corporation to the client's demat account.
Funds stay blocked in your own bank account until a trade settles, instead of being transferred to the broker upfront.
An exchange fund that compensates investors, within limits, when a broker defaults. NSE's ceiling is ₹35 lakh per investor.
Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation. It insures bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
Separating a defaulted bond into a separate portfolio within a debt fund, introduced by SEBI in December 2018 after IL&FS.
SEBI's online complaint system. Version 2.0, from April 2024, sets a 21 day resolution timeline.
A financial influencer on social media. SEBI-regulated entities cannot associate with unregistered finfluencers.

points: SEBI oversees markets and intermediaries, RBI oversees banks, lenders and money, exchanges run surveillance and settlement, and DICGC insures deposits
Regulators fight crises in two ways: firefighting with rate cuts, liquidity and trading halts, and rebuilding with new rules afterwards
After Karvy misused about ₹2,300 crore of client securities, reforms kept pledged shares in your demat, paid shares directly to you and let funds stay in your bank until trades settle
Deposit insurance rose 5 times to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank in 2020, with interim payment within 90 days if a bank is restricted
IL&FS led to side pocketing for debt funds and tighter NBFC regulation, and heavy F&O losses led to larger contract sizes, fewer weekly expiries and upfront premium collection
Regulators protect the market's plumbing, not your returns: bubbles, your own leverage and panic selling remain your responsibility

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment, legal or financial advice. Regulatory limits, timelines and rules described here reflect the position understood at the time of writing and change frequently. Always check the latest circulars on the SEBI, RBI, DICGC, NSE and BSE websites. References to specific firms describe publicly reported regulatory actions.
